title: History of the All England Club
sourceTitle: All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club is a private club in London. It is famous for the Wimbledon Championships. This is a tennis tournament played on grass. It takes place every summer.
pages.caption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

pages.text: The club was started by six men. At first, they only played a game called croquet. Later, lawn tennis became popular. The club added tennis courts, and tennis soon became the main sport played there.
pages.caption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

evidence.articleCaption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

pages.text: The club has many courts for players. There are grass courts, clay courts, and indoor courts. The grass courts are very important for the tournament. Workers take special care of the grass so it is always ready for the players.
pages.caption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

evidence.articleCaption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

pages.text: Over the years, the club had to close sometimes. It did not hold the tournament during the First and Second World Wars. It also had to cancel the event in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
pages.caption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

pages.text: Today, the club is known all around the world. It is run by members and a committee. People love to watch the famous grass court matches every year during the summer months in London.

B1-B2.headline: History of the All England Club

pages.text: Based in Wimbledon, London, the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club is a private members club. It is best known for hosting the Wimbledon Championships, which is the only Grand Slam tennis tournament still played on grass courts today.
pages.caption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

pages.text: The club was founded in July 1868 during a popular croquet craze. Originally called the All England Croquet Club, it was set up by six gentlemen. Lawn tennis was introduced to the grounds a few years later in 1875.
pages.caption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

evidence.articleCaption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

pages.text: Tennis quickly grew in popularity and soon became the main activity of the club. The first gentlemen's singles championship took place in July 1877. Croquet was dropped from the name for a period before being restored for sentimental reasons.
pages.caption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

evidence.articleCaption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

pages.text: The club moved to its current site in Church Road in 1922 because of the growing popularity of tennis. Centre Court was built that same year and has since been improved with new facilities, including a sliding roof added in 2009.
pages.caption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

pages.text: Throughout its history, the championships have faced several suspensions. The event was not held during World War I and World War II. In June 2020, the tournament was also cancelled for the first time since the war due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Today, the club maintains numerous courts, including eighteen tournament grass courts and practice areas at Aorangi Park. It continues to manage the historic grounds while keeping up with the modern demands of professional international tennis tournaments.

C1-C2.headline: Evolution of the All England Club

pages.text: Situated in the Wimbledon district of London, the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club operates as a private institution. Its primary renown stems from hosting the Wimbledon Championships, distinguished as the sole remaining Grand Slam event contested on natural grass.
pages.caption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court and No.1 Court in the background

pages.text: Established in July 1868 amid a regional croquet surge, the organization initially functioned under the name of the All England Croquet Club. Following the introduction of lawn tennis in 1875, the institutional focus shifted rapidly toward the emerging racket sport.
pages.caption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

evidence.articleCaption: People sitting on Aorangi terrace, better known as Henman Hill, watching main matches on the large screen

pages.text: By 1882, croquet was removed from the official title as tennis established dominance, though the older moniker was later reinstated for sentimental reasons. The inaugural gentlemen's singles championship was successfully conducted in July 1877.
pages.caption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

evidence.articleCaption: Aerial view of the grounds in 2022

pages.text: Growing public interest eventually necessitated a relocation to the current Church Road facility. This new site accommodated the newly constructed Centre Court, which has subsequently undergone substantial architectural modifications, such as the installation of a retractable roof.
pages.caption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

evidence.articleCaption: Centre Court with its retractable folding concertina roof

pages.text: Operational continuity has occasionally been disrupted by external crises. The championships experienced total suspensions throughout the durations of both World Wars, and more recently, the 2020 tournament was cancelled due to the global COVID-19 pandemic.

Contemporary facilities encompass numerous specialized surfaces, featuring multiple tournament grass courts alongside practice areas at Aorangi Park. The administration separates club membership management from the commercial operations of the annual championships.

title: The 2010 London Afghanistan Conference

pages.text: On 28 January 2010, leaders from many countries met in London. They came together at Lancaster House to talk about the future of Afghanistan. The meeting was hosted by the United Kingdom, the United Nations, and the Afghan government.
pages.caption: World leaders at the London Conference on Afghanistan, 28 January 2010

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Embassy London Photo / Public Domain

evidence.fileTitle: File:International Conference on Afghanistan (2010) world leaders.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: World leaders at the London Conference on Afghanistan, 28 January 2010

pages.text: The meeting brought together many important people. These included the Afghan president Hamid Karzai and the US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. They wanted to plan a new course for the country after years of conflict.

Before this meeting, the conference was planned for Kabul. Later, the location was changed to London. The United Nations and leaders expressed worries about security threats and rising attacks in Afghanistan.

At the conference, officials discussed important goals. Afghanistan agreed to timetables to take control of military and police functions. They also launched a program to help bring Taliban insurgents back to normal life.

President Karzai said foreign troops might still be needed to train Afghan forces for years. The international community might also need to give financial support to the army. A follow-up meeting was planned for Kabul.

On 28 January 2010, an international conference on Afghanistan took place at Lancaster House in London. The one-day event was hosted by the United Kingdom, the United Nations, and the Afghan government to chart a new course for the country.
pages.caption: World leaders at the London Conference on Afghanistan, 28 January 2010

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Embassy London Photo / Public Domain

pages.text: The meeting gathered foreign ministers and senior representatives from more than 70 countries. Attendees included Afghan President Hamid Karzai, US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and British Prime Minister Gordon Brown.

Although a summit was initially announced for Kabul, officials decided in late November 2009 to hold the meeting in London instead. Prior to the event, UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and the Security Council raised concerns over severe security threats.

During the conference, participants discussed transferring security responsibilities from international forces to Afghan forces. Officials planned to increase Afghan security forces to more than 300,000 by late 2010 or early 2011.

The government also launched a program with financial incentives to lure Taliban insurgents away from the conflict. President Karzai noted that foreign troops and financial backing might still be needed for several years.
Meanwhile, Iran criticized the conference as paternalistic and stayed away from the meetings. A follow-up conference was scheduled to take place later in Kabul to evaluate the progress made.

Initially proposed as a summit in Kabul, the venue was shifted to London in late November 2009. The conference convened against a backdrop of heightened security concerns, marked by a sharp rise in conflict-related incidents and civilian casualties.

Core objectives included drafting frameworks to transition security responsibilities from international forces to Afghan authorities. Plans were laid for Afghan security personnel to exceed 300,000 and for the government to assume territorial control incrementally.

Furthermore, the conference established mechanisms for reintegration and reconciliation, featuring an international fund to provide alternative livelihoods for insurgent fighters. Concurrently, debates arose regarding foreign aid disbursement and local governance performance.

President Karzai projected a prolonged requirement for foreign military training and financial assistance. Meanwhile, regional dynamics shifted as Iran boycotted the summit, criticizing the proceedings as an infringement upon national sovereignty.

title: Ancient Buddhist Rock Carvings of Manglawar
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Manglawar valley is a place in Pakistan. It is near the town of Mingora. This valley has many old Buddhist sculptures and rock carvings. People can see statues carved into big stones. The most famous one is the Shakhorai Buddha.
pages.caption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Aurel Stein wrote about the valley long ago. He saw many Buddhist rock reliefs. The biggest one is a seated Buddha. It is about thirteen feet tall. It is carved high up on a reddish rock wall above the narrow ground below.
pages.caption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: The large Buddha statue is very high up on the cliff. Because of this high place, it was saved from people who might have harmed it. But this same high place makes it very hard to take a good photograph of the statue today.
pages.caption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Researchers found many other rock carvings in the area. They are in places like Shaldara, Kalkata, and Banjot. Some stones show figures sitting or standing. Many of these old carvings are covered by thick plants, trees, and heavy natural patina.
pages.caption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: At Banjot, a round boulder shows different figures on its sides. One side shows standing and seated figures holding lotus flowers and water flasks. Water flowing over the rock has faded some of the artistic details over time.

B1-B2.headline: Ancient Buddhist Rock Carvings of Manglawar

pages.text: Situated in Pakistan about nine kilometers northeast of Mingora, the Manglawar valley features numerous Buddhist reliefs and sculptures. Among these ancient works, the best known is the colossal Shakhorai Buddha, located where several side valleys descend from the eastern watershed range.
pages.caption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: According to the accounts of Aurel Stein, the most striking carving is a seated Buddha about thirteen feet in height. It is carved on the vertical face of a reddish rock high above a narrow terrace. While this elevated position protected the relief from vandals, it makes photography difficult.
pages.caption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Some scholars believe the Swat Valley is the site of Oddiyana, a medieval kingdom important to Vajrayana Buddhism. The valley contains many sacred areas, rock reliefs, and inscriptions that once welcomed ancient pilgrims entering the region.
pages.caption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Recent discoveries have revealed further rock carvings in locations such as Shaldara, Kalkata, and Banjot. Many of these stones feature figures like Bodhisattvas in pensive attitudes. However, thick layers of patina, vegetation, and water channels have obscured several details.
pages.caption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: In Banjot, a round boulder displays multiple carved scenes across its exposed sides. These reliefs include figures holding water flasks and lotus flowers. Constant water flow across the rock surface has faded many of the intricate artistic details.

C1-C2.headline: Buddhist Sculptures and Carvings in Manglawar

pages.text: The Manglawar valley in Pakistan lies approximately nine kilometers northeast of Mingora at the convergence of side valleys descending from the eastern watershed. This geographic area preserves a dense concentration of Buddhist reliefs, sculptures, and inscriptions, anchored most famously by the Shakhorai Buddha.
pages.caption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Shaldara -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Historical accounts by Aurel Stein emphasize the archaeological significance of the valley, highlighting a colossal thirteen-foot seated Buddha carved onto a vertical reddish cliff face. Although this elevated location preserved the sculpture from pious vandals, it simultaneously impedes photographic documentation.
pages.caption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -1 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: The broader Swat Valley functioned as a sacred landscape containing numerous monasteries. Certain scholars propose it as the historical site of Oddiyana, a medieval kingdom associated with the dissemination of Vajrayana Buddhism and the homeland of notable sages.
pages.caption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -2 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: Beyond the principal site, archaeological surveys have documented new rock carvings across locations including Shaldara, Kalkata, and Banjot. These panels typically depict Bodhisattvas and other figures, though many surfaces suffer from severe weathering, obscuring patina layers, and vegetative overgrowth.
pages.caption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

evidence.articleCaption: Kalkata -3 Stupa, Manglawar

pages.text: At the Banjot site, a prominent boulder exhibits diverse engraved scenes featuring deities and Bodhisattvas holding attributes such as water flasks and lotus stems. Continuous water movement across the stone has progressively eroded these artistic details.

title: How election audits verify voting accuracy
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: After an election ends, people do a check called an election audit. This check helps to see if votes were counted correctly. It also shows if people followed the right rules. Election checks can look at the results or the process.
pages.caption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

evidence.articleCaption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

pages.text: Doing checks after an election is important. They help stop fraud and errors. But officials must finish these checks before they declare the final winner. If they only count votes by hand, redundancy helps make sure the work is accurate and safe.
pages.caption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

evidence.articleCaption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

pages.text: Using computers for elections can bring risks. Mistakes can happen if humans set up machines wrong. Machines can also break down or overheat. Sometimes hackers try to change computer software. This can happen on or before Election Day.
pages.caption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

evidence.articleCaption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

pages.text: Voting machines often get updates from flash drives. These drives can bring risks from the internet. Machines are sometimes left alone in public buildings at night. This makes it easier for people to access them.
pages.caption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

evidence.articleCaption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

pages.text: Checking votes has unique challenges. Banks can match money deposits to specific accounts easily. But election rules keep ballot choices private. Because of this, officials cannot link individual voters to their specific ballots.

B1-B2.headline: How election audits verify voting accuracy

pages.text: An election audit is a review conducted after polls close. Its main purpose is to determine whether votes were counted accurately or if proper procedures were followed. While quality management audits happen between elections, results audits must finish before declaring winners to protect against fraud.
pages.caption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

evidence.articleCaption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

pages.text: Jurisdictions that use manual hand counts build redundancy into their methods. This means multiple people view and confirm each vote, which can make separate audits unnecessary. However, computers introduce complex risks, such as software hacking, overheating, and unintentional human setup errors during elections.
pages.caption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

evidence.articleCaption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

pages.text: Voting machines are usually air-gapped from the internet, but they still receive updates through flash drives. Because these machines are sometimes left unattended in public buildings overnight, physical security becomes a major concern for election officials.
pages.caption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

evidence.articleCaption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

pages.text: Unlike banking systems that track individual accounts, election managers face strict ballot privacy rules. This privacy prevents officials from linking individual voters to their specific ballots, making standard financial audit practices impossible to use.
pages.caption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

evidence.articleCaption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

pages.text: Different states use various methods to check results. Some states require risk-limiting audits, which use independent computers and random hand checks of paper ballots to confirm totals. Recounts are also distinct, usually happening only when margins of victory are very close.

C1-C2.headline: The mechanics and challenges of election audits

pages.text: Post-election audits evaluate whether votes were tallied accurately or if established procedures were followed. While process and results audits serve quality management functions between cycles, results audits intended to deter fraud must conclude before official outcomes are declared.
pages.caption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

evidence.articleCaption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

pages.text: Manual tabulation methods inherently incorporate redundancy by involving multiple independent observers to interpret and verify votes. Conversely, computerized systems introduce vulnerabilities, including software manipulation by malicious actors, configuration errors, and hardware malfunctions like calibration loss or overheating.
pages.caption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

evidence.articleCaption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

pages.text: Although voting machines are frequently air-gapped, they remain susceptible to compromise via flash drives used for software updates. Furthermore, leaving machines unattended in public facilities prior to an election creates significant physical security vulnerabilities that outsiders can exploit.
pages.caption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

evidence.articleCaption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

pages.text: A fundamental challenge distinguishing elections from other IT applications is ballot privacy. Because anonymity prevents officials from associating specific voters with individual ballots, standard verification procedures utilized in financial institutions cannot be implemented.
pages.caption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

evidence.articleCaption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

pages.text: States employ diverse verification frameworks, ranging from routine sample hand counts to statistically rigorous risk-limiting audits. These risk-limiting procedures evaluate cast vote records against randomly sampled paper ballots to bound the probability of undetected outcome errors.

An election audit is a review conducted after polls close. Its main purpose is to determine whether votes were counted accurately or if proper procedures were followed. While quality management audits happen between elections, results audits must finish before declaring winners to protect against fraud.
pages.caption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

evidence.articleCaption: Boss Tweed: As long as I count the votes, what are you going to do about it?

pages.text: Jurisdictions that use manual hand counts build redundancy into their methods. This means multiple people view and confirm each vote, which can make separate audits unnecessary. However, computers introduce complex risks, such as software hacking, overheating, and unintentional human setup errors during elections.
pages.caption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

evidence.articleCaption: Most States Check Computer Counts Only on a Few Contests

pages.text: Voting machines are usually air-gapped from the internet, but they still receive updates through flash drives. Because these machines are sometimes left unattended in public buildings overnight, physical security becomes a major concern for election officials.
pages.caption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

evidence.articleCaption: Colorado elections in 2017, sample sizes needed for risk-limiting audits

pages.text: Unlike banking systems that track individual accounts, election managers face strict ballot privacy rules. This privacy prevents officials from linking individual voters to their specific ballots, making standard financial audit practices impossible to use.
pages.caption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

evidence.articleCaption: Ballots or scanned images available to public for independent audits

pages.text: Different states use various methods to check results. Some states require risk-limiting audits, which use independent computers and random hand checks of paper ballots to confirm totals. Recounts are also distinct, usually happening only when margins of victory are very close.

title: The Global History of Anti-Abortion Movements
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Anti-abortion groups are part of the abortion debate. They want to stop abortion and make it illegal. Many of these groups started after countries began to make elective abortions legal. Today, people in many nations still work to change laws and cultural views about this practice.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

pages.text: In France, the first anti-abortion group began in 1971. France has strict laws about when a woman can get an abortion. Later, the government allowed abortions in cases of distress up to ten weeks. After twelve weeks, it is usually a crime.
pages.caption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

evidence.articleCaption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

pages.text: In Ireland, several anti-abortion groups exist. The Irish constitution allowed for legal abortion in 2018. Even after this change, some anti-abortion political parties still campaign. Catholics and other groups also hold rallies and try to stop clinics.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

pages.text: Russia has legal abortion up to the twelfth week of pregnancy. The government passed new restrictions to help raise the birthrate. These rules include telling women about the dangers of abortion. Leaders and organizations also support national anti-abortion campaigns to raise awareness.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion advertisement on a truck in Vancouver in 2012

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion advertisement on a truck in Vancouver in 2012

pages.text: In the United States, modern anti-abortion groups grew after a major court decision in 1973. Some organizations focus on banning abortions at the state level. Activists also stand outside clinics to try to stop women from entering.

B1-B2.headline: The Global History of Anti-Abortion Movements

pages.text: Anti-abortion movements, which are also known as pro-life movements, participate in the ongoing debate against the practice and legality of abortion. Many of these organizations began as countermovements in direct response to the legalization of elective abortions in various countries around the world.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

pages.text: In France, the first specifically anti-abortion organization formed in 1971 during debates leading to the 1975 Veil Law. French law permits abortions up to ten weeks in cases of distress. After twelve weeks, unauthorized procedures are treated as serious crimes punishable by imprisonment and fines.
pages.caption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

evidence.articleCaption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

pages.text: Across Europe, laws vary significantly by country. In the United Kingdom, the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children formed when the 1967 Abortion Act passed. Activists in the UK still stand outside clinics to discourage women through prayer vigils and pavement counseling.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

pages.text: In the Republic of Ireland, several groups campaign against abortion despite a 2018 constitutional amendment providing for legal access. Meanwhile, Russian authorities enacted restrictions to combat a falling population, requiring providers to advertise health dangers and banning descriptions of procedures as safe.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion advertisement on a truck in Vancouver in 2012

pages.text: United States anti-abortion movements expanded significantly following the 1973 Supreme Court decisions. Organizations associated with conservatism and the Christian right continue to advocate for bans at state and local levels, while similar debates and protests occur in Canada and Australia.

Anti-abortion movements operate globally as active participants in legislative and cultural debates regarding the legality of abortion. Frequently self-styled as pro-life, these organizations often originated as direct countermovements following the legislative or judicial legalization of elective termination procedures in various jurisdictions.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion demonstration in Rome in 2019

pages.text: European legal frameworks exhibit substantial variation, ranging from parliamentary authorization to constitutional prohibition. In France, early organizational efforts accompanied legislation introduced by Simone Veil, establishing strict gestational limits and severe criminal penalties for unauthorized procedures. British legislation similarly regulates access through practitioner approval while maintaining potential criminal liabilities.
pages.caption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

evidence.articleCaption: "Each Life Matters" demonstration in Madrid in October 2009

pages.text: National contexts demonstrate diverse strategic approaches among anti-abortion entities. Irish organizations continue political campaigns despite a 2018 constitutional amendment legalizing abortion. In Russia, demographic concerns prompted legislative restrictions, obligating providers to disseminate health warnings and prohibiting descriptions of the procedure as safe.
pages.caption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

evidence.articleCaption: An anti-abortion protest outside an abortion clinic in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1986

pages.text: In North America, Canadian discourse increasingly emphasizes cultural persuasion and fetal personhood arguments, while private member bills attempt legislative restrictions. United States movements, galvanized by landmark judicial rulings, have intensified efforts at state and local levels following subsequent high court decisions regarding constitutional interpretations.

pages.text: Activist tactics frequently extend beyond conventional lobbying to direct engagement outside medical facilities. title: Understanding Global Dimming
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Global dimming is a reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth. It is caused by air pollution, especially sulfate aerosols. This decrease in solar energy was noticed when measurements started in the 1950s. Industrial pollution increased air particles, leading to less visible sunlight over the following decades.
pages.caption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.

evidence.articleCaption: Hotspots of sulfate aerosol pollution in 2005–2007 are highlighted in orange. Such sulfates rarely occur naturally outside of volcanic activity, and their increased levels are the main cause of global dimming.

pages.text: The sunlight dropped by four to five percent every ten years until the 1980s. Air pollution increased during these years because of post-war industrial growth. Solar activity did not change much during this period.
pages.caption: Satellite snapshot of atmospheric sulfur dioxide on 15 April 2017. Sulfur dioxide forms highly reflective sulfates, which are considered the main cause of global dimming.

pages.text: Aerosols have a cooling effect on the atmosphere. Global dimming has hidden the true extent of global warming. In the 1970s, heavily polluted regions even experienced cooling while the rest of the world warmed.
pages.caption: Early 2010s estimates of past and future anthropogenic global sulfur dioxide emissions, including the Representative Concentration Pathways. While no climate change scenario may reach Maximum Feasible Reductions (MFRs), all assume steep declines from today's levels. By 2019, sulfate emission reductions were confirmed to proceed at a very fast rate.
